Rather than learning the search geometry itself, TRACE makes the scale of chemical exploration explicit through a Tanimoto-similarity threshold controlling chemical extent and a cardinality budget controlling candidate-search breadth. A simple success/failure controller expands or contracts both quantities during optimization, while the GP and acquisition function select which admissible molecules to evaluate. Across six challenging molecular optimization benchmarks under matched 1,000-evaluation budgets, TRACE achieves the strongest overall sample efficiency as measured by the best molecule found as evaluations accumulate. Crossed ablations on two objectives further show that adaptive region control contributes beyond the proposal mechanism, while its benefit depends on the proposal distribution. We further apply TRACE to the stability of iron phthalocyanine (FePc), a non-precious molecular electrocatalyst whose degradation can involve loss of the Fe center. Using a first-principles density functional theory (DFT) workflow designed for accurate energy evaluation, TRACE increases the computed thermodynamic resistance to Fe dissolution from 0.42 to 2.59 eV over 80 designed evaluations.
entries.authors: Madhav R. Muthyala, Mahsa Askari, Farshud Sorourifar, Evan Zhou, Joe Gauthier, Joel A. Paulson

entries.title: Unmasking Four Knapsack Problems in the Traveling Thief Benchmark
entries.abstract: The traveling thief problem (TTP) asks a thief to choose a tour and a packing together, and the benchmark of 9,720 instances of Polyakovskiy et al. (2014) is the standard test set for comparing TTP heuristics. We show that four of these instances are not TTP instances at all. Their files give a renting rate of 0.00, so the tour has no effect on the objective and each instance reduces to a 0-1 knapsack problem. One of them belongs to the 60 categorized instances on which new methods are usually compared, and on it five of nine published methods report exactly the same value. The cause is the format of the files, which keep the renting rate with two decimals, while the rule of the generator gives a rate close to 0.003 on these instances. The same rounding may shift the rate of 949 other instances by more than 1%. Since the tour and the packing used by the generator were not published, the original rates cannot be recovered. We therefore define new rates with the same rule, applied to a fully specified reference solution that we publish, and we show with a published heuristic that the corrected instances behave as TTP instances again. We also give reference results on the corrected instances and recommendations for future studies. Finally, we present ttplib, a new open-source Python library that loads any of the 9,720 instances, including the corrected ones, without downloading the whole benchmark.
entries.authors: Mohammed Mizan Alanazi, Mahdi Khemakhem

entries.title: Converse Lyapunov theorem for input-to-state stability of infinite-dimensional systems
entries.abstract:
We prove converse Lyapunov theorems for input-to-state stability (ISS) of a broad class of infinite-dimensional systems applicable to evolution equations in Banach spaces, boundary control systems, and delay systems. To this end, we employ a novel method that does not require constructing auxiliary closed-loop systems. We start by showing that ISS of a control system implies uniform global asymptotic stability of the same system with respect to trajectory-dominated inputs. Then, under an additional regularity requirement, we prove that an ISS Lyapunov function can be constructed.
  Based on our general result, we prove that for linear systems with unbounded $\infty$-admissible operators, ISS is equivalent to the existence of a Lipschitz continuous coercive ISS Lyapunov function.
entries.authors: Patrick Bachmann, Andrii Mironchenko

entries.title: Double Blind Evals: Resolving the Dual Confidentiality Dilemma in AI Safety Auditing
entries.abstract: AI safety evaluations often involve sensitive prompts and proprietary models. Evaluators want to keep their evaluation prompts secret from model owners to prevent purposeful or incidental data leakage, ensuring longer usefulness of their benchmark. Model owners in turn wish to keep their proprietary model weights and inference code within their own secure infrastructure to protect their IP. We present a way forward for "double-blind evals", which provide cryptographic guarantees that an evaluator's prompts are not shared with the model owner, while simultaneously maintaining the confidentiality of the model weights and inference code. To accomplish this, we use secure enclaves that encrypt data in RAM at the hardware level. In a world-first pilot, we test this approach by evaluating a proprietary Google DeepMind model (Gemini 2.5 Flash Lite) against a selection of the private AILuminate benchmark corpus, using an NVIDIA H100 secure enclave on Google Cloud Platform, and using OpenMined's PySyft to maintain data and model privacy. We believe this effort marks the first use of this technology to provide mutual secrecy for one organization's frontier-class proprietary model weights and another organization's closed benchmark.
entries.authors: Andrew Trask, Sol Messing, Vai Pahwa, Pegah Maham, Rene Kolga, Austin Frantz, Andrew Tash, Kate Thomas, Sean McGregor, George Balston, Patricia Paskov, Miles Brundage, Akriti Vij, Bennett Hillenbrand, Alexandros Karargyris, Tin Acosta, Joel Fenster, Madeleine Elish, Rasmi Elasmar, Myriam Khan, Koen van der Veen, Rasswanth S, Sameer Wagh, Stephen Gabriel, Pedro Werneck, Lacey Strahm, Kevin McDonough, Ronnie Falcon, Kristian Lum, William Isaac

entries.title: Diophantine conditions for absolute continuity of projections for self-similar measures
entries.abstract: We prove that every projection of a planar self-similar measure $\mu$ is equivalent to Lebesgue measure on its support if the rotations satisfy a simultaneous Diophantine condition with exponent $\tau$ and $\mu$ has finite $s$-energy for some $1+2\tau\le s<2$. Under strong separation, we prove the fibre measures have exact dimension $\dim_H\mu-1$. For self-similar sets $E$ with $\dim_H E>1+2\tau$, the same rotation condition implies uniformly positive projection lengths and fibres of dimension $\dim_H E-1$ at Lebesgue-almost every point of each image without separation assumptions. The absolute continuity and fibre dimension theorems extend to non-coordinate projections of products under a joint Diophantine condition with exponent $\tau$ on the logarithmic contraction ratios. These imply for all self-similar sets $K,L\subset\mathbb R$ satisfying this condition and $\dim_HK+\dim_HL>1+2\tau$, every sum $uK+L$, $u\ne 0$, has positive length, and $\dim_H(L\cap(y-uK))=\dim_HK+\dim_HL-1$ for Leb. a.e. $y\in uK+L$. The proof combines the $L^1$ Gaussian smoothing approach used in the higher dimensional case with averaging at random stopping scales with a Brownian martingale bound using It\^{o} calculus.
entries.authors: Xiong Jin, Tuomas Sahlsten

entries.title: Graph-Guided Bayesian Factor Analysis: A Fast Integrated EFA-CFA Approach for High-Dimensional Data
entries.abstract: Factor analysis has been central to the analysis of high-dimensional biomedical data. However, existing exploratory and confirmatory factor analysis methods face several limitations: less interpretable factor findings, difficulty in identifying which variables can and cannot be represented by low-dimensional factors, challenges in estimating the covariance among factors, and maximum-likelihood fits that break down when variables outnumber subjects. We propose graph-guided Bayesian factor analysis (gg-BFA) to address these gaps. We first use a Bayesian model to explore and learn the latent graph structure, identifying which variables can and cannot be represented by low-dimensional factors and how many factors are needed. A dense-subgraph search proposes partitions of the variables into communities, each defining one factor, and a forward stepwise search compares their fractional variational posteriors and stops when the evidence lower bound first decreases. We show that this search recovers the true communities even when the number of variables grows much faster than the sample size. We then develop a confirmatory Bayesian model whose variational posterior of the covariance contracts at the parametric rate up to a logarithmic factor, yielding posterior inference for the factors and their covariance, as well as predictions of missing values. Its four members range from a community mask to several cross-loadings per variable. In five biomedical panels, the complete analysis took under ten minutes each on one GPU, and cross-loadings improved held-out covariance and the prediction of masked measurements. In TCGA Kidney, six of the first eight factors were enriched for known pathways, and 190 of the 210 factor correlations had 95% credible intervals excluding zero. Overall, gg-BFA is computationally fast and provides interpretable factor analysis findings and reliable inference results.
entries.authors: Shitao Fan, Lizhen Lin, Zhenyao Ye, Shuo Chen

entries.title: A Dual-Frequency-Constrained Structure-Function Kirchhoff Model for Near-Nadir Ocean Backscatter -- Part I: Theoretical Framework
entries.abstract: Most operational near-nadir geophysical model functions (GMFs) are empirical and fitted one radar band at a time, and do not explain the difference between Ku and Ka band. This paper derives a backscatter model in which one local description of the sea surface serves both bands. The near-nadir Kirchhoff integral is written in terms of the elevation difference between two surface points separated by a horizontal lag. The surface then enters through the structure functions of that difference, and the scattering kernel selects the lags each band samples, about 2.5-1.4 cm at Ku and 1.0-0.5 cm at Ka band. Geometric optics is recovered as the quadratic, isotropic limit, without a spectral cutoff. With a logarithmic second-order structure function, one wind-dependent log-slope sets both the incidence shape and the Ku-Ka shape difference, and band transfer reduces to evaluating one curve at a second lag. Same-footprint dual-frequency radar data show that one band alone does not determine this transfer. The log-slope is the level of the short-wave saturation range and grows about as the square of the wind speed; a physical short-wave spectrum reproduces this growth but overestimates the level. Dual-frequency radars thus measure the centimetre-scale roughness level, although they do not separate a scale-dependent structure function from non-Gaussian surface statistics. A companion paper delivers and evaluates the resulting GMF, KuKa-Mod.
entries.authors: Alexey S. Mironov, Fr\'ed\'eric Nouguier, Bertrand Chapron

entries.title: Spike-to-Field Mechanisms of Turbulence-Like Dynamics in Spatial Spiking Neural Networks
entries.abstract: Neural avalanches and turbulence-like brain dynamics are usually measured after neural activity has been coarse-grained into continuous fields, leaving open which spike-level mechanisms can generate these macroscopic observables. We build a spatial leaky integrate-and-fire spiking neural network and explicitly transform spikes into activity-density and Hilbert phase fields. A delayed, distance-dependent, passive-dendrite regime reproducibly generates turbulence-like field structure, including high-amplitude phase-defect tracks, structure-function scaling, and power-law-favored continuous-field avalanche tails. Controls show that firing rate, vortex count, and avalanche tail fits are individually insufficient: destroying delayed propagation, dendritic filtering, or spike timing suppresses key field signatures, while random-space nulls can retain many mathematical phase defects but show weaker spatial structure and synaptic-delay transfer. Biologically motivated gates further shape the regime: PV-like perisomatic inhibition clamps phase dynamics, SST-like dendritic inhibition and projection-specific inhibitory facilitation preserve long-lived tracks, and a rate-constrained projection-STP regime expresses a roughly 200-ms episode at 12.25 Hz (full-record mean) across 12 seeds. These results use SNNs as a mechanistic testbed for spike-derived brain turbulence observables and show why phase defects and avalanche-like statistics must be interpreted jointly with spatial scaling and spike-level propagation.
entries.authors: Zequan Liu

entries.title: Adapting Small Language Models to Romanized Nepali: Tokenizer Fertility, Reference Likelihood, and Generation Metrics
entries.abstract: Romanized Nepali, Nepali written in Latin script, is common in digital communication but has no standard spelling and few resources, and it is unclear how reliably small open language models can be adapted to it. We adapt three 2-3B base models from different families, Llama-3.2-3B, Qwen2.5-3B, and Gemma-2-2B, with QLoRA on 9,000 instruction examples produced by deterministic transliteration of Nepali instruction data. Each model is trained with one shared recipe and three seeds and evaluated on 1,000 held-out examples with reference-overlap metrics, byte-normalized reference likelihood (bits per byte, BPB), and an output audit, against zero-shot baselines under two prompts. Fine-tuning raises chrF++ from 10-14 to 29.0-30.6 and lowers BPB from 2.23-2.41 to 0.78-0.84; most zero-shot outputs (54-92%) are English-like. Likelihood and overlap disagree on how far apart the models are. Llama-3.2-3B has the lowest BPB in every seed, 0.042 below Qwen2.5-3B (95% CI 0.039-0.046), yet the two cannot be separated on chrF++ (30.51 and 30.61) or BLEU, even with paired item-level tests. Gemma-2-2B, whose tokenizer splits Romanized Nepali words least (2.72 tokens per word), scores worst on every measure. Which model gains most over its zero-shot baseline depends on the zero-shot prompt. In a supplementary comparison with an identical tokenizer, Llama-3.1-8B lowers BPB by 0.053 (0.050-0.056) relative to Llama-3.2-3B, while chrF++ and BLEU rise by only 0.68 and 0.58 points. Lower fertility and higher reference likelihood therefore did not identify the model whose outputs were closest to the references.
entries.authors: Pujan Pant, Sagar Newpane, Hari Sitaula, Manish Sakhakarmy

entries.title: How Far Does Second-Order Linear Response Predict Quantization Mismatch? Pre-Registered Measurements on Five Language Models
entries.abstract: Serving systems choose a weight format for each model and deployment. A low-cost screen predicts the resulting KL divergence from the unquantized model's Fisher information using $\tfrac12\Delta^\top F\Delta$, the expansion underlying Hessian-aware and second-order post-training quantizers. We assess the reliability of this screen in GPU batches with channel-wise int8, per-tensor fp8 and group-wise int4 on Qwen3-8B, Qwen3-4B, OLMo-2-7B, Qwen3-32B and Qwen3-30B-A3B. Relative predictions hold across a 16-fold range of perturbation scales, int4 group sizes and rounding modes, while absolute predictions are heavy-tailed. A trimmed average brings 10 of 12 cells on Qwen3-4B and OLMo-2 within 15% of measured KL. The MoE model exhibits nonquadratic response at small perturbations, with int8 KL scaling as $\alpha^{0.63}$. Computing per-sequence gradients in bf16 can cause fourfold prediction errors. We trace these errors to arithmetic in the lower half of the backward pass and eliminate them by using fp32 there. Batch-invariant kernels run at 0.55 times the throughput, while changes in reduction order introduce a floor of 0.17-0.22 nats per sequence. We build a screener with one streamed fp32 Fisher pass, trimmed tensor-block predictions with a band, a flag for aligned tensors and per-layer format allocation. On the unseen Mistral-7B-v0.3 family, all six predictions fall within the band, all three KL budgets are met, and vLLM throughput is predicted within 0.4%.
entries.authors: Dezhen Lu, Zixiang Ni

entries.title: Beyond Sunny Skies: Using Large Language Models to Predict Urban Traffic in Adverse Weather
entries.abstract: Urban traffic flow prediction is a cornerstone of intelligent transportation systems, yet accurate forecasting under adverse weather conditions remains a significant challenge. Existing data-driven models, while effective for routine patterns, often struggle with the sparse data and complex non-linear shifts associated with rare meteorological events. These methods typically treat environmental contexts as shallow numerical features, failing to capture the underlying semantic reasoning-why and how specific adverse conditions alter mobility behaviors across regions with different functional compositions. To address this limitation, we propose Multi-STG, a unified framework that integrates Large Language Model (LLM)-derived semantic priors with graph-based spatiotemporal learning. Multi-STG introduces an LLM-empowered semantic enhancement module that transforms comprehensive context descriptions such as weather, POIs, and holidays into high-level semantic embeddings, effectively providing a knowledge-driven complement to data scarcity. Furthermore, we design a multimodal attentional fusion mechanism to dynamically weigh heterogeneous inputs and a semantic-enhanced prediction head with gated residual calibration to robustly adjust forecasts based on semantic guidance. Extensive experiments on real-world multi-city private car datasets demonstrate that Multi-STG outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, reducing MAE by 11.82\% on average relative to the strongest baseline across three cities, while maintaining stable performance under sparse and non-stationary conditions.
entries.authors: Zhu Xiao, Kuan Feng, Tong Li, Chenxi Liu, Gang Wang, Zhuo Tang, Kenli Li

entries.title: TrialDesignBench: Benchmarking Language Models for Phase-I Trial Design Against Clinical Knowledge
entries.abstract: AI is used in much of the clinical trial pipeline. However, selecting the statistical design of a trial, a crucial step that determines how drug doses are tested on humans and evaluated, has seen almost no AI progress. LLMs appear to be a natural fit given their strengths in biomedical knowledge and statistical reasoning. Nevertheless, there is currently no appropriate way to evaluate such abilities because recent regulatory and methodological shifts, most notably FDA's Project Optimus, have redefined what constitutes a reasonable design and rendered many previous designs obsolete. To lay the groundwork for AI-assisted trial design, we introduce TrialDesignBench, a benchmark of 617 Phase-I/I-II oncology dose-finding trials, each paired with an expert-validated reference design that is consistent with the latest FDA regulatory initiatives. This reference standard is produced through a formalization of the expert design process. We evaluate five frontier LLMs, none of which matches the reference standard. Our ablation experiments trace this performance gap to two main causes, inference of latent, unrecorded design determinants from trial sources (supplying them raises class-wise balanced accuracy by 0.22) and structured decision-tree reasoning (+0.24). TrialDesignBench offers a reproducible, contemporary-standard objective for evaluating and enhancing AI-assisted trial design.
entries.authors: Yihan Hank Tang (University of Pennsylvania), Peng Yang (The University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center), Jiayi Xin (University of Pennsylvania), Tianqi Shang (University of Pennsylvania), Xuyang Chen (University of Pennsylvania), Ying Yuan (The University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center), Yi Lian (University of Pennsylvania), Qi Long (University of Pennsylvania)

entries.title: Simulation-aided Reinforcement Learning with Control Variates
entries.abstract: Reinforcement Learning (RL) algorithms often rely on data collected from a target environment, which can be expensive and noisy. Although simulators can generate large amounts of additional data, standard simulation mixing approaches, which directly combine simulated and real experience, can degrade performance due to simulator inaccuracies, especially when they bias the solution away from the optimal policy. We propose a conservative simulation-aided learning method based on control variates, where simulated data is used solely to reduce variance in the learning process rather than directly shaping the learning target. We develop our approach for Policy-Evaluation, which is a fundamental building block of RL algorithms. Then we combine it within the actor-critic framework towards policy improvement, as well as extend it towards offline RL scenarios. Experiments on multiple MuJoCo benchmark tasks demonstrate improvements over standard simulation mixing approaches, highlighting control variates as an effective tool for simulation-aided reinforcement learning.
entries.authors: Omer Hemo, Ido Sefi, Mirco Mutti, Aviv Tamar, Kfir Y. Levy

entries.title: A Dual-Frequency-Constrained Structure-Function Kirchhoff Model for Near-Nadir Ocean Backscatter -- Part II: The Practical GMF, KuKa-Mod
entries.abstract: Near-nadir radars, from altimeters and rain radars to wave scatterometers, need a geophysical model function (GMF) relating backscatter to wind, yet most operational models are empirical and specific to one band. This paper delivers KuKa-Mod, an operational near-nadir GMF for wind retrieval at Ku and Ka band, built on one physical description of the sea surface, and evaluates it. Following the companion paper (Part I), the additive coefficient and log-slope of a logarithmic surface structure function are fitted jointly to the Ku-band incidence profile of the Global Precipitation Measurement (GPM) radar and to the same-footprint Ku-Ka shape difference. The model reproduces the Ku profile and reaches the azimuth-averaged Ka profile with no additional shape parameter and one fitted level, largely explained by the seawater dielectric and the clear-sky attenuation. Against scatterometer winds the Ka-Ku difference holds to within 0.3 dB up to 25 m/s, whereas the near-nadir Ka wind sensitivity is about 20% too weak. An empirical correction measured against the same winds sets the operational high-wind level of both bands, validated to 20 m/s. Without a sea-state coefficient, a long-wave tilt predicts where the response to significant wave height changes sign at Ku band, a tilt that CFOSAT/SWIM confirms, and the azimuth harmonics are reproduced once a sensor-dependent offset is removed. The operational model is released as parameters, an evaluator and look-up tables ready for retrieval processors.
entries.authors: Alexey S. Mironov, Fr\'ed\'eric Nouguier, Bertrand Chapron

entries.title: Certify, Report, or Refuse: Harm-Constrained Conformal Prediction for Clinical Actions
entries.abstract: Routing a melanoma case to routine follow-up is a serious action error that diagnostic coverage alone does not rule out. We present Harm-Constrained Risk-Optimal Conformal Prediction (HC-ROCP), a training-free framework that uses frozen classifier probabilities and adds a harm penalty when choosing prediction sets and actions. We test the resulting policies on disjoint calibration splits with multiplicity adjustment. HC-ROCP certifies supported claims, reports descriptive fallback policies, and refuses unsupported subgroup claims. We evaluate these outputs retrospectively on COVID-19 radiographs, ISIC 2019 dermoscopy, and EyePACS-to-APTOS retinopathy transfer. Across ten calibration seeds, HC-ROCP reduces COVID-19 severe-action errors from the exact risk-optimal baseline's 4.68\% to 0.54\%. At a 5\% budget, global claims are certified for COVID-19 and ISIC, but the rare squamous-cell-carcinoma claim is refused. At 1\%, all settings receive descriptive reports. For each budget, we also report the minimum severe-case count needed to pass the global harm gate with zero errors, providing a starting point for further data collection.
entries.authors: Zhiyuan Li, Lequan Yu

entries.title: Trade Promotion Optimisation for Consumer Goods
entries.abstract: Trade promotions consume a large share of consumer-goods revenue, yet most planners still set discounts with a single, often unreliable, price elasticity per item. We present an end-to-end Trade Promotion Optimisation (TPO) system built as one chain: analogue SKUs, point elasticity, elasticity curve, price recommendation, promotional lift and net lift. Elasticity is measured at post-promo time from directional price-dip events against a rolling regular price, and at promo time by a causal estimator that residualises trend, seasonality and promotion, handles stock-out censoring with a Tobit likelihood and updates itself from the first clean promotion week. Items with weak evidence borrow the point elasticity and the curvature from analogue SKUs chosen by a cross-validated ridge model over category, brand, sub-category, price line and description. The optimiser separates self-price lift from substitution and post-promo dips and adjusts for inventory and trade funding. In a four-week promotion experiment on a 39-SKU consumer brand (mean elasticity -3.06), the plan lifts units by 20.6% and revenue by 6.9% at flat margin. Analogue pooling halves elasticity error relative to hierarchy averaging.
entries.authors: Ankur Verma, Namrata Gupta

entries.title: Controlled Binary Assignment Flows
entries.abstract: This paper introduces a geometric approach to the representation and learning of time-variant parametrizations of deep assignment flows, for binary data labelings on graphs. Each edge carries an optimally controlled parameter flow in a 2-dimensional totally geodesic submanifold, based on objectives derived from a non-local linear scale space representation of the input data. The aggregation of triplets of such flows in 5-dimensional totally geodesic submanifolds is learned from data. The fusion of these flows determines the trajectory in the high-dimensional symmetric parameter space and by geometric integration the layers of binary deep assignment flows. Numerical results demonstrate the expressivity and the limitation of our highly parallel geometric local synthesis approach to high-dimensional deep assignment flow parametrizations.
entries.authors: Paul Fr\"ohling, Christoph Schn\"orr

entries.title: Interpretability Is Not Model-Specific
entries.abstract: Interpretability tools are usually built for one model at a time: a refusal direction, a truthfulness probe, or a steering vector is found with labeled data inside the model it explains. We ask whether such tools can be carried to other models through a map between residual streams fit only on unlabeled prompts. We transfer a refusal direction, tested causally by addition and ablation, and two read-out tools, a correctness direction and a sentiment probe, across 110 pairs of models from five families and 1B to 72B parameters and between base and instruction-tuned models, with controls for specificity and five seeds. How much transfers depends on what the map was fit on. A map fit on ordinary questions recovers 54\% of the target's own refusal steering and 16\% to 77\% of its correctness gain; adding unlabeled prompts from the region where the tool operates raises these to 102\% and 88\% to 98\%, while control directions recover at most 1\%. We prove that a linear map behaves this way whenever two models correspond linearly on the data it covers, and a label-free coverage score derived from this result tracks recovery across more than 16,000 runs and explains earlier reports that maps between models fail across domains. Carried read-out tools outperform anything the target's unlabeled representations yield. Interpretability results, once found, can be reused across models at the cost of a few unlabeled prompts.
entries.authors: Marcus Armstrong, Navid Ayoobi, Pradham Mummaleti, Alexander Chulzhanov, Arjun Mukherjee

entries.title: VLA Adaptation with Real and Simulated Data: A Case Study on Robotic Chess
entries.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models are trained as general-purpose foundation models for robot learning, and require fine-tuning for each downstream task and robot. This raises practical questions such as how much data and training updates are needed, how checkpoints should be selected, and whether simulation can be leveraged to alleviate the cost of real data collection. We study these questions on a task that requires both precise manipulation and spatial understanding of the scene. In this task, an SO-101 arm moves a chess king between two squares that are given only by their names, such as e4 and a5. We fine-tune $\pi_{0.5}$ with various dataset sizes and update budgets, using teleoperated demonstrations as well as simulated demonstrations from a randomized scripted expert that imitates the variability of human demonstrations. In simulation, the success rate scales with both data and updates. Importantly, we find that a short learning-rate cool-down adds up to 31 points and is necessary for comparing checkpoints, and that validation loss and action error are unreliable for model selection. On the real arm, we fine-tune on up to 256 teleoperated demonstrations and evaluate ten policies in 25 trials each. Partial results indicate that pretraining on the simulated demonstrations helps substantially, most clearly when real data is scarce. We also present a negative result, in which training on the policy's own rollouts with filtered behavior cloning, RECAP-style advantage conditioning, corrections from an automatic coach, or residual reinforcement learning did not yield a measurable improvement over plain behavior cloning in our setting. We release the simulator, the expert and the real demonstrations.
entries.authors: Mat\v{e}j Kripner, Milan Straka

entries.title: Library of Hands: Fix the Hands, Not the World Model
entries.abstract: A world model predicts how a scene changes after an action, and a planner uses it to search for actions that reach a goal. If the camera moves or the controller changes, the same command moves the robot differently: when its commands are turned by 90 degrees, a frozen planner with the LeWM world model that succeeds in 77.5% of episodes succeeds in only 7.8%. Current fixes retrain the model, need training data, or forget a set-up when it returns. We propose Library of Hands (LoH), a training-free method that keeps the world model frozen and corrects only the map from commands to applied actions, which we call the hand. LoH reads the hand through the frozen model, with no extra sensor: it finds the action that best explains the change between two camera images (a reading). It stores every hand it identifies, so a returning set-up is recognised rather than re-learnt. In closed-loop tests, LoH more than doubles success on three simulated tasks, from 28.6% to 62.3%, and loses only 0.6 percentage points when nothing changes. It also works, unchanged, with two other world models and on two of three models pretrained on real robot data, and its gain grows with the quality of its readings.
entries.authors: Hasaan Ahmad, Qizhen Ying, Yuxuan Sun, Tianjin Huang, Guangming Wang

entries.title: A four-step validation protocol for radiomic survival analysis in small cohorts: a body composition case study
entries.abstract:
Gastroenteropancreatic neuroendocrine tumors (GEP-NET) lack prognostic biomarkers, and computed tomography (CT)-based body composition radiomics at the third lumbar vertebra (L3) is a promising candidate. Small cohorts make high-dimensional radiomic models prone to overfitting and single-split evaluations variable and optimistic.
  This methodological study proposes a four-step validation protocol for radiomic survival analysis in small cohorts: (1) false discovery rate (FDR)-corrected feature selection, (2) a dual-path comparison of prior feature selection versus embedded regularization, (3) repeated nested cross-validation (CV) and (4) a negative control with Gaussian noise features. In 78 GEP-NET patients, 535 radiomic features from five L3 compartments were used to evaluate five survival models with Harrell's concordance index (C-index), time-dependent area under the curve (AUC) and integrated Brier score (IBS).
  Step 1 selected at least one feature in 18% of outer folds under noise (nominal level 20%) versus 84% with radiomic features. The dual-path comparison showed no consistent difference between strategies. Repeated nested CV reduced variability across seeds (41% median reduction in C-index standard deviation), but not enough to distinguish models. The nested CV C-index exceeded chance by 0.07-0.15 with radiomic features but not clearly under noise (0.40-0.42 with prior feature selection, 0.47-0.55 with embedded regularization). Frequently selected features tentatively linked greater subcutaneous fat, skeletal muscle compactness and texture to better prognosis.
  These findings suggest a modest prognostic signal in L3 radiomics, with considerable uncertainty that the protocol quantifies. The protocol may transfer to other small-cohort radiomic survival studies. Code: https://github.com/marielatalaveram/radiomics-survival-validation-protocol.
entries.authors: Mariela Talavera-Mu\~noz, Cecilia Diana-Albelda, Miguel Antonio Sampedro-Nu\~nez, Victor Rodriguez-Laval, Jesus Bescos, \'Alvaro Garc\'ia-Mart\'in

entries.title: reComposer: Editable Planning for Controllable Image Generation
entries.abstract: Prompt-based image generation makes it easy to produce visual assets, but offers little support for engaging with the creative process. Prompting collapses interdependent creative decisions into a monolithic instruction and returns a finished image, leaving control limited to revising the prompt or correcting the model's output. We present reComposer, a process-oriented image-generation interface built around editable planning, which decomposes users' evolving intent into meaningful creative decisions - such as subject, composition, or palette - and collaborates with users to explore underspecified goals and alternatives. reComposer supports conversational and direct manipulation of the plan, moving between concept-level intent and visual-level control. We evaluated reComposer with 8 design and non-design professionals. Compared to prompting, participants felt greater control and ownership while developing visual assets, exploring alternatives, and iterating on details. Our findings suggest how shifting generative AI interaction from specifying outputs to shaping process can support creative thinking alongside asset production.
entries.authors: Susie S. Y. Li, Angie Boggust, Fred Hohman, Donghao Ren, Dominik Moritz, Yannick Assogba

entries.title: CoilStellaration: A Dataset and Benchmark for Engineering-Aware Stellarator Coilset Generation
entries.abstract: Stellarators are fusion devices that use externally generated, three-dimensional magnetic fields to confine hot plasma and offer a promising route to commercial fusion. Their electromagnetic coils pose a challenging design problem: they must reproduce the target magnetic field while satisfying engineering constraints and remaining practical and cost-effective to manufacture. Finding suitable geometries is a highly nonlinear inverse problem that generally has neither a closed-form nor a unique solution. This problem lies at the heart of stellarator design. We introduce CoilStellaration, a dataset and benchmark for learning the mapping between coil geometries from target plasma magnetic fields and engineering requirements. The dataset contains 177,000 optimized filamentary coilsets targeting plasma equilibria from ConStellaration, with sampled engineering requirements and achieved geometric and magnetic-field metrics. It spans multiple coil counts and field-period numbers, supporting studies of both specialized and shared models across configurations. The benchmark asks models to predict coils conditioned on a target equilibrium and requirements on coil-coil and coil-plasma spacing, curvature, and magnetic-field error. We show that magnetic-field accuracy remains the main challenge, with learned models rarely satisfying all requirements simultaneously. However, using learned predictions to initialize conventional coil optimization can accelerate early progress. We release baseline models and evaluation code to support reproducible research on both direct coil generation and learned optimization initializations. By lowering the barrier for machine learning and optimization researchers to engage with stellarator coil design, we aim to accelerate progress toward practical, cost-effective stellarator power plants.
entries.authors: Jan-Hendrik Ewers, Santiago A. Cadena, Nicol\`o Foppiani, Andrea Merlo

entries.title: Average versus expected causal effects under interference: Modeling assumptions and estimation bottlenecks
entries.abstract: Causal inference under treatment interference requires assumptions to reduce the exponentially large number of potential outcomes. We develop hierarchical finite-population models for potential outcomes by separating these assumptions into three layers: interference neighborhoods, exposure mappings, and outcome models. Given an interference neighborhood and exposure mapping, we show that potential outcomes admit a nonparametric decomposition into direct, spillover, and treatment--spillover interaction components. This decomposition provides a common coordinate system for nonparametric, semiparametric, and parametric models of finite-population potential outcomes. For a given potential-outcome model, we define two classes of estimands. Average causal effects (ACEs), such as direct and total treatment effects, contrast potential outcomes under fixed treatment--exposure conditions. Expected causal effects (ECEs), such as expected direct and indirect effects, contrast expectations of potential outcomes under a specified allocation policy. For both classes, we bound the variance of the canonical Horvitz--Thompson estimator by three terms: a diagonal weight term, a term from overlapping interference neighborhoods, and a residual design-dependence term. Our upper and lower bounds show that under graph-unaware designs, nonparametric design-unbiased estimation of ACEs can require sample sizes growing exponentially in the interference degree, whereas polynomial growth can suffice for design-aligned ECEs. Under neighborhood interference, we construct graph-aware independent-set designs with variance bounds polynomial in the maximum degree for direct and total treatment effects on every graph, whereas graph cluster randomization can incur worst-case variance exponential in the degree.
entries.authors: Vishesh Karwa, Edoardo M. Airoldi, Donald B. Rubin

entries.title: Agnostic Marginal-Nonuniform Learning
entries.abstract:
We study the problem of binary classification in the marginal-nonuniform learning framework in the agnostic setting. In this model, the constants in the learning rate may depend on the marginal distribution of the unlabeled data, but the guarantee must hold uniformly over all conditional distributions of the labels. We also study fine-grained rates.
  We consider two criteria.
  (1) The standard agnostic setting, where the learner competes with the best concept in the class. In this setting, an immediate consequence of standard agnostic PAC learning results gives us the optimal rate of $\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{n}}$ for every class $\mathcal{H}$ with finite $\mathrm{VC}(\mathcal{H})$ and shows that arbitrarily slow rates are necessary otherwise. This also gives us the optimal fine-grained rate of $\sqrt{\tfrac{\mathrm{VC}(\mathcal{H})}{n}}$. Therefore, the dependence on the marginal distribution does not help, which is in contrast to the realizable setting.
  (2) In the relaxed agnostic setting, where the learner competes with $(1+\lambda)$ times the error of the best concept for a fixed $\lambda \in (0,1]$, the picture from the realizable setting reappears. We obtain a trichotomy of the achievable optimal rates: exponential rates of the form $e^{-n}$ arise precisely when the class is finite; linear rates of the form $\tfrac{1}{n}$ arise when the class is infinite but $\mathrm{VC}(\mathcal{H})$ is finite; and arbitrarily slow rates occur when $\mathrm{VC}(\mathcal{H})=\infty$. We also obtain the optimal fine-grained rate of $\tfrac{\mathrm{uVCE}(\mathcal{H})}{\lambda n}$, where $\mathrm{uVCE}(\mathcal{H})$ is a recently introduced combinatorial complexity dimension called the uncentered $\mathrm{VC}$-eluder dimension.
entries.authors: Tanmay Devale, Steve Hanneke, Amirreza Shaeiri

entries.title: TACTUS: A Robotic Palpation System for Spatially Heterogeneous Hardness Mapping of Woody Breast Myopathy
entries.abstract: Woody breast (WB) myopathy is a spatially heterogeneous fibro-degenerative condition of the broiler Pectoralis major muscle. Existing mechanical reference methods rely on single-point or sequential compression measurements, limiting characterization of spatial hardness variability. This study presents TACTUS (Tactile Adaptive Conformal 3D Uniform Sensing), an automated tactile array that generates thickness-normalized, three-dimensional hardness maps at 20 anatomically distributed locations within approximately 30 s. TACTUS integrates 20 independently motorized tactuators with force-sensing resistors and encoder-driven linear actuators, alongside a LiDAR depth camera for surface profiling and adaptive compression. The system was evaluated using 100 broiler breast fillets across four WB severity classes (Normal, Mild, Moderate, Severe). TACTUS identified significant force differences among severity classes (ANOVA, p < 0.001), with the strongest differentiation in the cranial region and a significant caudal effect not detected by texture-analyzer measurements. Fillet-level TACTUS force showed moderate but significant correlation with texture-analyzer measurements (Pearson r = 0.441, p < 0.001). Semivariogram, local change entropy, and heterogeneity analyses revealed increasing and anatomically structured hardness variability with WB severity. These findings demonstrate TACTUS as an automated, operator-independent platform for spatially resolved mechanical characterization and ground-truth generation to support hyperspectral and near-infrared spectroscopy-based WB classification systems.
entries.authors: Chaitanya Pallerla, Yihong Feng, Avisekh Tripathy, Yang Tian, Pouya Sohrabipour, Amirreza Davar, Casey M. Owens, Cengiz Koparan, Dongyi Wang

entries.title: Generalized Adaptive Boosting and the Geometry of Mistakes
entries.abstract: Not all mistakes are alike. For example, in medical diagnosis, false positive and false negative mistakes have a different impact and should not be aggregated. By revisiting the classical theory of boosting through this lens, we introduce the notion of $Z$-learner, which returns weak hypotheses achieving joint false-positive/false-negative guarantees $(\mathrm{FP},\mathrm{FN})$ from some set $Z \subseteq [0,1]^2$. This formulation generalizes the standard notion of $\gamma$-weak learning--recovered by taking $Z=\{(z_1,z_2): z_1+z_2<1/2-\gamma\}$--and allows for more flexible notions of weak learnability that account for the impact of the distribution on the achievable learning guarantees. This raises a natural question: which sets $Z$ are boostable? We answer this by giving a complete geometric characterization that unifies, as special cases, both the classical boosting dichotomy and the recent multi-objective extension of Bressan et al. (COLT 2025). We also present an adaptive algorithm for boosting $Z$-learners without relying on the prior knowledge of $Z$, generalizing AdaBoost's ability to handle unknown margin parameters. Finally, we demonstrate that $Z$-learners can achieve confidence amplification. However, the analysis is significantly more involved than in classical boosting and relies on the centerpoint theorem from discrete and computational geometry.
entries.authors: Marco Bressan, Nataly Brukhim, Nicol\`o Cesa-Bianchi, Emmanuel Esposito, Yishay Mansour, Shay Moran, Maximilian Thiessen

entries.title: GeoScope: Training-Free Program Execution beyond the Counting Horizon for Ultra-High-Resolution Remote Sensing Question Answering
entries.abstract: In ultra-high-resolution (UHR) remote sensing images, the objects that questions count in a region or relate by direction often span only a few pixels. Existing methods mainly decide where a vision-language model (VLM) should look and trust its answer in the chosen view. We show that this assumption fails for counting, and measure VLMs as one calibrates a sensor. All eight open VLMs tested fall increasingly short once a view holds more than a certain number of objects, about five for most on DOTA aerial images. This counting horizon narrows as views grow and objects appear smaller. An empirical power-law response model predicts the undercount a split recovers and the spurious counts it adds, and supports the rule of splitting only views beyond the horizon. In GeoScope, a text-only language model parses the question into a typed spatial program that fixes the region and its resolution. The VLM only grounds and counts within its operating range, and directions are computed explicitly from the grounded boxes. To our knowledge, it is the first UHR method to split views by a measured limit of the VLM. Without training, it improves Qwen3-VL-8B by 16.3 points on regional counting and 10.5 on spatial relations in XLRS-Bench, and has the highest reported accuracy, trained methods included, on regional counting and on the whole benchmark by question. On UHR-Micro it improves global and regional counting by 16.8 and 36.2 points, 15.6 of the former from splitting. On MME-RealWorld counting it gains 11.4 points, and we show that an option that is almost never correct yet often chosen distorts comparisons there. Project page: https://avalon-s.github.io/GeoScope/
entries.authors: Guohui Deng, Yuhang Jiang, Chengjun Wang, Zhongwen Hu, Zhaocong Wu, Linsheng Huang, Jinling Zhao, Chao Ruan, Miaozhong Xu, Chi Chen

entries.title: Fisher-Glass Learning: Classification Bounds and Subpopulation Audits
entries.abstract: Accurate classifiers can fail when background cues change without altering the correct labels. Predictive performance alone does not quantify how much task information remains after accounting for such nuisance variation. Here we extend the Fisher-glass framework to connect nuisance-adjusted information with local classification difficulty and subpopulation auditing. We derive lower bounds on local minimax excess classification risk under explicit distinguishability and decision-separation conditions, alongside statistical audits accounting for estimation error and regularization. On Waterbirds, a feature-based diagnostic of task-background alignment selects an accurately classified group, with selection frozen before held-out evaluation. Across five training seeds, background replacements preserving the extracted bird foreground and labels yield 93.2% accuracy when background type is preserved and 40.6% when it changes, a controlled difference of 52.6 percentage points. Separately, search using task labels and a fixed nuisance direction identifies an independently evaluated population with 98.8% membership-weighted accuracy and low estimated projected predictive Fisher information. Training and acquisition experiments show that information gains and predictive gains can diverge. These findings support joint assessment of predictive performance, information under declared nuisance models and controlled sensitivity when diagnosing vulnerability and evaluating model improvements.
entries.authors: El Mustapha Mansouri

entries.title: Multi-Agent Screening: What Agreement and Acceptance Cannot Tell You
entries.abstract: When AI agents screen items for a costly human assessor, as in agentic search, e-discovery and AI reviewing of papers, only what they pass gets judged. We show what each kind of evidence can establish about their errors, even with unlimited data. Agreement shows that agents concur, not that they are right, however many there are. Acceptance by the assessor gives precision but only a lower bound on recall. Knowing which agents found which relevant items gives an upper bound on recall if agents' finds are not negatively correlated, and caps what one more agent can add if agents are interchangeable. Without assumptions about the agents, recall can be pinned down only by judging items they did not pass: a random sample of these estimates how many relevant items were missed, to any chosen accuracy, and the sample needed does not grow with the number of agents.
entries.authors: Benjamin Chang, Dell Zhang

entries.title: Hidden Tails: Certifying Tail-Risk Claims under Selective Labels
entries.abstract: Historical decisions determine which outcomes are observed, potentially concealing a predictor's largest errors. Even unlimited data from the same observation process can therefore leave population tail risk unresolved. Here we derive sharp bounds on conditional value-at-risk, the average loss in a specified upper tail, for binary outcomes and bounded losses. These bounds span exactly the risks compatible with the observations and a stated limit on how outcome odds differ between observed and hidden cases at the same covariate values. Under stated regularity conditions, calibrated statistical certificates cover these ranges simultaneously across candidate predictors, supporting risk limits and model comparisons while separating statistical uncertainty from persistent ambiguity. For a fixed predictor and loss threshold, we derive a minimum-cost allocation for reducing excess-loss ambiguity by prioritizing hidden outcomes according to ambiguity removed per unit cost. This allocation treats audited population contributions as known and retains the original sensitivity bounds separately for audited and still-hidden outcomes. In controlled masking experiments with known loan repayments, recovering about 16% of hidden labels removes a median 61% of estimated fixed-threshold ambiguity, compared with 16% for random recovery. These results connect population tail-risk claims to the available evidence and identify where additional outcomes can sharpen their assessment.
entries.authors: El Mustapha Mansouri

entries.title: Hidden frequencies in topological dynamical systems
entries.abstract: We show for certain skew products built over any infinite minimal nilsystem, the frequencies present in the nilsystem are not always enough to govern recurrence for the whole system. This strengthens and generalizes a theorem of Glasscock, Koutsogiannis, and Richter.
entries.authors: Seljon Akhmedli

entries.title: Scaling Taxonomy-Free Image Labeling with Generative AI: A Multimodal
entries.abstract:
Providing real-time multimodal insights into images is challenging because it requires low latency, high description accuracy, and scalable solutions that are both cost-effective and efficient. For example, given a new image of an outfit, we would like to generate insights that the image depicts "earth tones" and "linen pants" and allow users to explore similar ideas along these themes. Traditional strategies to generate such insights would typically involve building taxonomies producing a golden set labeled by humans, training models on these datasets, and deploying these models for online inference services. Such workflows are constrained by fixed taxonomy, high labeling cost, limited labeling coverage in sample space, and human errors and expertise gaps in labelers. In addition, these methods are expensive and cumbersome to iterate over time. Recent trends have started exploring generative AI models for online insights, but this method suffers from long latency and prohibitive costs to support a high volume of requests or large amounts of offline labeling needs.
  We present Generative Labeling On Clusters (GLOC) as a solution to provide highly scalable, cost-effective, low latency, and high accuracy online image insight services. GLOC leverages highly optimized image embeddings to form image clusters that are semantically close to each other for the purpose of the type of insights, and summarizes the insights at the cluster level, which effectively generalizes to members in the cluster. At Pinterest, GLOC powers image descriptors and pivot query suggestions for Hybrid Search, which is a multimodal search service enabling users to search with both an image and a text query. Our offline and online A/B tests demonstrate that GLOC significantly outperforms previous methods, delivering improvements in quality and efficiency.
entries.authors: Zhenjie Zhang (Irene), Sainan Chen (Irene), Kshiteesh Hegde (Irene),  Mengze (Irene),  Li, Pouya Rezazadeh Kalehbasti, Munachim Ezema, Karina Sobhani

entries.title: Residual-Based Spectral Submanifold Reduction of Constrained Multibody Systems on Matrix Lie Groups
entries.abstract: The parameterization method yields efficient and accurate reduced-order models for nonlinear dynamical systems, but existing procedures that compute them assume polynomial vector fields on vector spaces. Constrained multibody systems instead obey differential-algebraic equations on matrix Lie groups such as $\mathbb{R}^3 \times SO(3)$ and $SE(3)$. Minimal parameterizations of these groups lead to non-polynomial equations that must be approximated or recast before reduction, and current implementations require the nonlinearities as explicit multilinear maps, which are cumbersome to construct for assembled multibody systems. This work develops a parameterization framework for constrained multibody systems on matrix Lie groups. Rigid and floating frame of reference bodies use rotation-matrix components or Euler parameters, while geometrically exact beam elements use an Euler-Rodrigues representation that eliminates the logarithmic map and expresses the exponential map polynomially, retaining screw-motion interpolation. The reduced-order models satisfy linear joint constraints exactly, and a rotation-preserving parameterization keeps the configuration on the Lie group to machine precision. The parameterization method is formulated directly in terms of the assembled residual, so that only residual evaluations and their derivatives are required. Truncated Taylor arithmetic delivers all Taylor coefficients of a given order from a single residual evaluation, and a non-intrusive coupling to codes with real-valued residuals is demonstrated with the multibody code Exudyn. Numerical examples show accurate prediction of backbone curves, forced response curves, and internal resonances at substantially reduced computational cost.
entries.authors: Stefan Holzinger, Tiago Martins, Daniel Rixen

entries.title: OptiCover: A Scalable and Multi-Surface Framework for Cold-Start Visual Optimization under Semantic Constraints
entries.abstract:
Selecting an effective cover photo is a critical yet understudied problem in visual merchandising for e-commerce marketplaces. On Airbnb, hosts upload many photos depicting different rooms, amenities, and points of interest, but must manually choose a single static cover photo that is reused across heterogeneous product surfaces. This creates substantial challenges: over 90\% of listing photos have no engagement labels, leading to a severe cold-start regime; guest preferences vary across surfaces and search intents, and visually captivating photos may be semantically misaligned with the underlying listing. At Airbnb scale, this corresponds to hundreds of millions of photos and hundreds of thousands of new uploads per day.
  We propose \emph{OptiCover}, a scalable framework for cold-start visual optimization under semantic constraints and multi-surface engagement signals. The framework combines (i) a photo candidate generator that identifies candidate photos through various proxies, (ii) lightweight vision heads applied to frozen CLIP embeddings for large-scale semantic scoring, (iii) a cross-modal grounding validator based on a vision-language model (VLM) that enforces semantic representativeness, and (iv) an Exploration Logging Module (ELM) that orchestrates the collection of randomized engagement data across heterogeneous product surfaces and contextual search intents.
  We evaluate OptiCover through extensive offline studies and multiple online experiments across HomePage, and Search surfaces. OptiCover is now deployed in production and performs tens of millions of photo swaps daily. Online results show a 1.5\% engagement lift on the HomePage and a 0.35\% increase in bookers on Search, generating millions of dollars in incremental revenue. Our findings suggest that action-space shaping and semantic constraints are primary drivers of performance.
entries.authors: Guillaume Guy, Mihajlo Grbovic, Joe Mills, Selen Uguroglu, Liwei He, Pratiksha Kadam, Nalini Kartha, Qian Aria Li

entries.title: Safe Reinforcement Learning for Multi-Turn Clinical Agents: When Dense Rewards Beat Outcome Rewards
entries.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards is increasingly used to improve language model reasoning, yet its effects on sequential decision procedures remain poorly understood. We study this problem in clinical multi-turn agents that must decide what information to request, when to stop gathering evidence, and which action to take. We introduce three controlled environments: medication refill triage, acute diagnostic work-up, and dosing titration, each with hidden clinical states, query costs, exact adaptive oracles, and deterministic outcome verifiers. Across these tasks, outcome-only group relative policy optimization often improves aggregate reward while producing undesirable procedures, including premature commitment, one-question collapse, and failures on rare high-risk cases. In diagnostics, assigning dense credit to questions that reduce uncertainty improves held-out value and moderate-case support across three training seeds relative to outcome-only reinforcement learning, without the high-risk seed collapse observed under outcome-only training. Separating exploration from exploitation further increases high-risk support at its best checkpoint, but at the cost of excessive information gathering on low-acuity cases. Additional experiments show that the optimal strength of process credit is task-dependent; that after a supervised warmup that already gathers carefully, reinforcement learning raises aggregate reward by trimming questions while degrading high-risk performance; and that reinforcement learning does not reliably repair rare behavior gaps inherited from biased supervised data. Verifiable final outcomes are therefore insufficient for training reliable multi-turn agents: reward design must account for the procedure used to reach an answer, and evaluation must distinguish adaptive information gathering from reward-exploiting shortcuts.
entries.authors: Brendan P. Murphy, Agustina Saenz

entries.title: KiteNorm: Variance Regularisation for Stable and Scalable Post-LN Transformers
entries.abstract: Post-LayerNorm Transformers have seen limited practical adoption due to enduring difficulties in scaling them to large depths. While prior research has focused on stabilising Post-LayerNorm by improving conditioning at initialisation, stability often deteriorates when models are trained with large learning rates, forcing additional compromises. In the decoder-only settings we study, existing Post-LayerNorm methods fail to outperform strong Pre-LayerNorm baselines. We propose KiteNorm, a post-norm training method designed to break this trend by constraining hidden-state variance. This approach is motivated by a bound on the LayerNorm Jacobian suggesting that variance growth contributes to gradient vanishing, alongside empirical evidence linking it to rank collapse. KiteNorm combines residual scaling and variance regularisation to maintain stability throughout training, supported by scalarised double-normalisation that provides separately learnable scales for the skip and residual branches. Across decoder-only Transformers up to 1.3B parameters, KiteNorm improves training stability and outperforms leading baselines at their optimal learning rates, with scaling laws favouring KiteNorm across depth, width, batch size, and training budget. Ablations show that each component is necessary for the full stability and performance gains.
entries.authors: Leon A. Trochelmann, Sajad Movahedi, Shiwei Liu, Antonio Orvieto

entries.title: $\Sigma$-LeWM: Learning World Models via S-Information for Robot Control
entries.abstract: World models have increasingly been applied as a model-based control method for robotics tasks such as manipulation and locomotion. While early world model architectures relied on decoders to prevent mode collapse and learn a predictable latent space, recent works on world models, such as Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture or LeWorldModel, increasingly aim to learn embeddings without a grounding decoder, utilising only a latent forward dynamics predictor and a stabilising entropy term. In this paper, we set out to demonstrate that the further introduction of two additional latent losses to LeWorldModel, a backward dynamics predictor and an inverse dynamics action predictor, enforces further structure on the latent embedding, leading to further gains in both performance and planning efficiency. These are critical properties for improving the applicability of such methods to real-time model-based control of real-world robots. We demonstrate these gains on standard world model benchmarks and two simulated robot manipulation tasks.
entries.authors: Xinrui Zu, Michael Przystupa, Zhao Yang, Shujian Yu, Kevin Sebastian Luck

entries.title: Finite temperature and pressure structural relaxations including zero-point motion and anharmonicity
entries.abstract: At finite temperature and pressure, the equilibrium structure of a crystal minimizes the Gibbs free energy rather than the static Born-Oppenheimer energy. We present WARP (Wyckoff-constrained Anharmonic Relaxations at Pressure and temperature), a symmetry-constrained, variable-cell relaxation based on the stochastic temperature-dependent effective potential method, including anharmonicity and zero-point motion. Every position update is projected onto Wyckoff positions and every strain onto symmetric strains, so a relaxation can raise the symmetry but never lower it. For aluminum, the thermal expansion follows measurements at cryogenic temperatures, including the quantum plateau below 50 K. For lanthanum hydrides at megabar pressures, equations of state agree with phonon-based and path-integral calculations, and LaH$_{10}$ relaxes from its rhombohedral static minimum to the observed cubic phase, also with a machine-learned potential fine-tuned on 150 supercells. For brucite, Mg(OD)$_2$, lattice parameters, bond distances and thermal expansion agree with neutron diffraction, and the O-D isotope effect is captured.
entries.authors: Henricus R. A. ten Eikelder, Florian Knoop, Florian Trybel

entries.title: Inference Validation for Regulated AI: Building a Decision Pipeline on NVIDIA AIPerf
entries.abstract: Deploying large language models in regulated industries requires more than picking the fastest inference engine: it requires evidence that a configuration meets contractual and legal obligations before it serves a single customer request. We describe Runway, an internal validation harness built at MasterControl that builds a governed decision pipeline around NVIDIA AIPerf. The key insight is separating concerns: AIPerf provides the trusted measurement, while Runway provides the experiment design that comes before it and the compliance, cost, and audit decisions that come after. We describe the architecture and the storage model that makes caching and audit one mechanism. We report three findings from Runway sweeps: TensorRT-LLM and vLLM rankings invert with concurrency; a newer, pricier GPU instance can be the cheaper one per request; and speculative decoding behaves differently across engines under load, so engine configuration can outweigh engine choice.
entries.authors: Dev Akre, Roman Bobalo, Manoj Dobbali

entries.title: Periodic vortex dipoles near closed geodesics on Riemannian surfaces
entries.abstract: We study the motion of a pair $(p_1,p_2)\in\Sigma\times\Sigma$ of point vortices with equal magnitude and opposite signs on a closed oriented Riemannian surface $(\Sigma,g)$. Given a closed geodesic that satisfies a non-degeneracy condition we construct a one-parameter family of periodic solutions $(p_1^\varepsilon,p_2^\varepsilon)$, $0<\varepsilon<\varepsilon_0$, of the Hamiltonian dynamical system for point vortex pairs whose trajectories converge towards the geodesic curve. The two vortices lie on opposite sides of the geodesic, are separated of order $\varepsilon$ and have period $2\pi\varepsilon$. The proof is based on a differentiated expansion of the Riemannian distance in Fermi coordinates, an augmented Lyapunov--Schmidt reduction, and an intricate contraction argument in scaled variables. The reduced normal equation is governed by the Jacobi operator of the closed geodesic, and the first order correction to the normal center of the dipole is characterized by an inhomogeneous Jacobi equation involving the curvature and the regular part of the Green function of the Laplace-Beltrami operator.
entries.authors: Thomas Bartsch, Angela Pistoia

entries.title: Clique Constraints for Exact Causal Structure Learning
entries.abstract: Exact score-based causal structure learning supports explicit structural constraints and optimisation certificates, but its branch-and-cut search can be computationally demanding. We augment exact causal structure learning methods with an upper bound on the maximum clique size of the learned undirected skeleton, enforced at integer candidates through lazy cycle and clique constraints. On static linear-Gaussian Erd\H{o}s-R\'enyi and scale-free DAGs, we evaluate callback order, alternative clique-cut policies, incumbent repair, fractional separation, and Big-M bounds. We report causal-recovery metrics jointly with optimality gaps, primal and dual bounds, node throughput, MIPSOL events, and callback cost. Two variants receive particular attention: B3 selects the most violated minimal (k+1)-clique inequality at each callback, whereas C3 repairs an infeasible integer candidate by deleting violating edges and refitting affected regression columns using QR-based least squares. The results do not indicate that clique constraints uniformly accelerate optimisation. However, their benefit depends on graph density, sample size, and cut-management policy, while large collections of correlated constraints can reduce node throughput. Tighter valid Big-M bounds reduced the fixed-budget optimality gap in most tested settings, without necessarily changing SHD or F1 at a fixed time limit. These findings characterize the computational trade-offs of clique-constrained exact causal learning, and identify selective separation and incumbent repair as promising directions.
entries.authors: Xiaoyu He, Pavel Ryt\'i\v{r}, Petr Ry\v{s}av\'y, Jakub Mare\v{c}ek

entries.title: The Narrative Gap: Can LLMs Help Us Navigate Diverse Narratives Across Languages?
entries.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly mediate how people seek and consume information, including accounts that differ across languages and regions, especially on contested topics. Supporting diverse information seeking requires models to help users navigate competing narratives across languages and information streams. We define six capabilities necessary for diverse multilingual information seeking: three foundational capabilities for narrative inclusion, narrative exclusion, and missing narrative identification; and three higher-level capabilities for presenting diverse narratives, preserving narrative coverage under confirmatory queries, and maintaining information parity across languages. To guide the development of those information seeking capabilities, we introduce \textsc{NarrativeBench}, a benchmark comprising 1,333 news articles in 23 publication languages across 23 contested topics and 460 Reddit-grounded queries. Evaluating 14 LLMs across 24 query languages, we find that current models lack the capabilities needed to reliably navigate diverse narratives, limiting users' control over the perspectives they receive and leaving substantial gaps in exposure to competing accounts even when diversity is explicitly requested. Information access also differs across query framings and languages, risking echo chambers, linguistic filter bubbles, and information disparities that weaken the common ground needed for democratic discourse. \textsc{NarrativeBench} provides a foundation for developing information systems that give users across languages and regions agency to navigate diverse narratives.
entries.authors: Nikhil Sharma, Kelly Marchisio, Kenton Murray, Ziang Xiao

entries.title: From Granger causality to causal structure in dynamical systems
entries.abstract: The idea of testing whether the past of one signal improves the prediction of another can be traced back to Wiener. It was Granger who formalized the concept. Granger causality has become one of the most widely used tools to infer directed interactions between the components of a system. The name however can be misleading: it detects predictive relations among the measured signals, not causal relations among the mechanisms that generate them. This article starts by reviewing recent advances in observation-space Granger analysis. It then follows a path to directed structure in latent dynamical models, and asks under which conditions that structure can be read causally.
entries.authors: V\'ictor Elvira

entries.title: DeepChronos: Temporal Neuro-Symbolic Reasoning for Multi-Step Attack Detection
entries.abstract: Modern cyber threats commonly unfold as multi-step attacks comprising temporally and causally related phases. Current defenses commonly follow a detect first and correlate later paradigm. Intrusion detection systems classify events independently, while downstream systems reconstruct attack progression from the resulting alerts or audit records. In this context, learning-based detectors learn attack-step dependencies implicitly as statistical regularities in the data and cannot guarantee that their predictions follow the real attack progression. Conversely, correlation systems represent attack relationships explicitly, but apply this knowledge only after the underlying attack observations have been detected. We present DEEPCHRONOS, a neuro-symbolic network intrusion detection system that shifts the paradigm from detect first and correlate later to detection through logical progression. DEEPCHRONOS combines learned flow-level evidence with explicit attack-phase rules, temporal prerequisites, and previously inferred phases, allowing the evolving attack history to inform and constrain each detection decision. Evaluations on DARPA 2000 and AIT-LDS V2 show that DEEPCHRONOS improves macro F1 over purely neural baselines by up to 11.3%, eliminates causal violations under strict temporal constraints, and maintains millisecond-scale inference latency. These results demonstrate that integrating explicit attack progression knowledge into detection produces more accurate and temporally coherent multi-step attack predictions.
entries.authors: Sofia Burkow, Andrea Agiollo, Enkeleda Bardhi, Fernando Kuipers, Kaitai Liang, Georgios Smaragdakis

entries.title: Sage-Taiyi: A Metacognitive Architecture for Scientific Discovery
entries.abstract: We introduce Sage-Taiyi, a metacognition-inspired architecture that uses accumulated scientific understanding to guide what to investigate next and how to investigate it. Through explicit monitoring and control, the system revises its understanding of evidence, assumptions, and unresolved questions, then uses these assessments to adapt research targets and select reusable reasoning methods. On Taiyi-Bench, an AI co-scientist ideation benchmark comprising 265 tasks from 50 papers across ten disciplines, Sage-Taiyi ranks first on all eight metrics of historical rediscovery and open-ended ideation, achieving an Overall score of 54.0 compared with 47.9 for the strongest baseline, AI Scientist-v2. It also performs well on two external scientific ideation benchmarks. Five expert-guided collaborations further connect its proposals to experimental and computational validation across chemistry, materials science, and engineering. In chemistry, reaction-condition optimization raises the yield of cobalt-catalyzed carbonylation from trace amounts to 84% and photocatalytic allylic amination from 13% to 69%. These results support metacognitive regulation as an approach to scientific ideation and its progression toward practical validation.
entries.authors: Weida Wang, Benteng Chen, Yigeng Jiang, Shuchen Pu, Weiping Shen, Zichao Liu, Yulin Su, Zitong Wang, Siyu Zhou, Zifu Wang, Yizhi Li, Xin Zong, Yuning Yang, Jixiang Bi, Yuan Wang, Chuyi Peng, Shiyao Geng, Qi Zhang, Kuan Lu, Mengzhu Li, Weiwang Xu, Peishan Xiang, Chengjun Liu, Chengrui Wei, Fangchen Yu, Shengji Tang, Yichen Jiang, Jingqi Ye, Cheng Yang, Tao Hu, Jianbiao Mei, Qinglong Cao, Kun Li, Yixin Chen, Shengyuan Xu, Juncheng Xiao, Yiheng Wang, Ruizhe Chen, Shiyang Feng, Runmin Ma, Xiangchao Yan, Zongsheng Cao, Haomeng Hu, Yu Ke, Taihui Wu, Meng Dai, Xu Guo, Haoyang Peng, Yinglong Ni, Pingsen Shi, Xiaosong Wang, Shuyue Hu, Haijun Li, Sherry Dongqi Bao, Yang Yang, Chao Yang, Jie Hou, Tianfan Fu, Yi Gong, Jin Zeng, Mao Su, Hongxia Hao, Fanyang Mo, Fenghua Ling, Tianshu Yu, Yunqi Cai, Baihong Chi, Jingwei Wang, Lei Wang, Chuncheng Bu, Shide Lv, Guangyu Wang, Yuqiang Li, Chunfeng Song, Lei Bai, Hui Wang, Xujun Fu, Li Cao, Lei Chen, Dahua Lin, Xing Xie, Bowen Zhou, Wenlong Zhang, Pinlong Cai, Peng Ye, Aiwen Lei, Jie Li, Shengchun Wang, Bo Zhang, Shufei Zhang

entries.title: PORT: Preference Optimization via Robust Token-Level Reweighting
entries.abstract: Preference optimization has become a central approach for aligning large language models with human values, but its effectiveness depends heavily on the quality of preference annotations. In practice, preference data is often noisy due to annotation errors and ambiguity. Existing robust preference optimization methods primarily operate at the sequence level, implicitly treating entire responses as uniformly correct or incorrect. However, rejected responses may still contain informative reasoning steps, while preferred responses can include subtle errors. In this work, we propose \textbf{P}reference \textbf{O}ptimization via \textbf{R}obust \textbf{T}oken-level reweighting \textbf{(PORT)}, a fine-grained framework for robust alignment under noisy preferences. PORT performs token-level reweighting using the empirical cumulative distribution function (CDF) of token log-probabilities, yielding an efficient forward-pass-only proxy to gradient-norm penalization that selectively suppresses corrupted tokens without additional backward-pass computation. We provide theoretical analysis showing that PORT reduces the gradient bias from noisy preference labels by minimizing an upper bound on the bias term. Extensive experiments across diverse noise settings demonstrate that PORT consistently improves robustness and outperforms existing sequence-level baselines. The code is available at https://github.com/osu-srml/PORT
entries.authors: Ding Zhu, Xiukun Wei, Tian Xie, Zhihui Zhu, Xueru Zhang, Mohammad Mahdi Khalili

entries.title: Learning Rate Decay Can Exponentially Accelerate SGD for Global Optimization of Nonconvex Functions
entries.abstract: Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) is a workhorse algorithm for continuous optimization. It is a folk belief among deep learning practitioners that learning rate decay in SGD substantially improves performance. However, it has remained unclear whether learning rate decay offers an asymptotic advantage for global nonconvex optimization. We answer this question in the affirmative by demonstrating a natural class of nonconvex functions for which, we prove that SGD with learning rate decay requires exponentially fewer gradient queries for global optimization than SGD with any fixed learning rate in the small-step size regime. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first exponential advantage that has been demonstrated for learning rate decay. The class of functions we consider includes many popular benchmark nonconvex functions. Our results provide a robust explanatory theory for the empirically observed benefits of learning rate decay for global optimization. We show that annealing performs the non-logconcave sampling task associated to the optimization problem in polynomial time, via a novel application of weak Poincar\'{e} inequalities.
entries.authors: Guneykan Ozgul, Dylan Herman, Junhyung Lyle Kim, Shree Hari Sureshbabu, Shouvanik Chakrabarti

entries.title: LogCDM: Interpretable Log Anomaly Detection via Behavioral Graph Drift and Adaptive Signal Fusion
entries.abstract: Log-based anomaly detection is increasingly dominated by large pretrained models, from BERT-scale encoders to 8B-parameter language models, which require GPUs at inference time and are difficult to deploy on the monitoring nodes where logs are produced. We present LogCDM, a compact detector that scores each log session using three complementary signals: the next-event surprise of a small causal Transformer, the distance between a graph-attention embedding of the session's own transition graph and that of a normal reference graph, and a transition-drift statistic that we show is exactly a frequency-weighted chi-squared divergence between transition kernels. The divergence view yields an asymptotic null distribution, a length-standardized score, and a per-edge decomposition that explains each alarm. A sigmoid gate fuses the three signals; under a shared-covariance Gaussian model, this gate is the Bayes posterior, and its learned weights indicate which signal each dataset relies on. With 8.1-8.8M parameters and no GPU required at inference, LogCDM reaches F1 scores of 0.984 on HDFS, 0.870 on chronologically split BGL, and 0.850 on Thunderbird, within 0.013-0.12 of an 8.1B-parameter LLM detector evaluated under the same protocol and above all compact baselines on BGL. It scores a session in 5.5-10.5 ms on a CPU. Ablations show that the structural signals add 0.025-0.030 F1 on BGL and Thunderbird but almost nothing on HDFS, consistent with the learned fusion weights.
entries.authors: Suryansh Talukdar, Taha Sarwat, Jin Soung Yoo

entries.title: Anchor Behavior, Not Parameters: Rehearsal-Free Continual Learning with a Single Shared Prompt
entries.abstract: Prompt-based continual learning adapts a frozen pre-trained vision transformer by tuning a small set of prompt tokens. Recently, one-prompt methods which share one single prompt across all tasks make this paradigm maximally parameter efficient. The open question is how a shared prompt can keep the knowledge of old classes while being updated for new ones. Existing methods protect old knowledge in parameter space, where they freeze task-specific prompts, expand new components, or sparsely gate which tokens receive gradients. However, this method sacrifices plasticity, yet the drift it still permits in shared tokens can corrupt the prompt's function on past classes. What must be preserved is the prompt's behavior.
